title: TomorrowNow Technical Demonstration | AI for Food Security Forum
transcriptText:
Hey everyone. Um, my name is Brian
Miranda, and I'm the CEO of TomorrowNow.
And so, what you see behind me is our
North Star vision, 100 million weather
resilient farmers across Africa.
And with all the recent advances in AI,
I think we've got a real shot of getting
there. Um, so, um, what we are looking
at is transforming the decisions that
farmers make every day.
Um, the decisions that, um, dictate
success or failure with every harvest.
And so, um, weather uncertainty is one
of the biggest drivers of food security,
or food insecurity, across Africa today.
Um, and this is not just the big shocks,
the droughts, the floods, the heat
waves. Um, these are the micro shocks,
or the changes, uncertainty, that happen
every single day. Um, the reality is 90%
of African smallholder farmers are
rain-fed.
That means they don't have irrigation,
and weather drives pretty much
everything that they do. So, every
decision they make, from when to plant,
what to plant, all the way down to when
to harvest, is largely driven by the
weather.
And the first question we get asked
every time we speak to farmers is, "When
will the rains come?" And so, this is
Maggie. Um, she's a farmer in Nakuru
County, in Kenya. And she said, um, the
following when we met with her earlier
this year.
"If you plant early, the harvests are
usually good.
But if you plant late, there are
challenges."
And she ultimately relies on guesswork
to decide when to plant every season.
And that's the, again, the reality for
most farmers today.
And, um, where we're missing the mark,
where most advisory and guidance happens
today, is at the the county level, uh,
even broader. Um, where, um, it doesn't
actually match up to the local
conditions that most farmers are
experiencing on the ground.
And so, um, when you look at, um, Nakuru
County here, there's lowlands,
highlands, different soil types,
different weather patterns. Um, in, um,
the reality is for for two different
farmers, the same event of early rains
can mean something very different. So,
early rains can be a false start or an
opportunity. So, on a false start, you
know, the rains might come in and then
stop. There's a dry spell for many days
and you've planted the seeds, but they
don't germinate. They don't take root
and and ultimately, you're left with
diminished crop yield.
On the other hand, if you're able to
capture the rains, the rains sustain,
then you get to a place where um, you
capture the full growing season. And so,
a difference of even a couple of weeks,
two weeks, can reduce yield by 10 to
30%, which is dramatic for for many
farmers. And most farmers can control
the timing of when they plant. So, this
is a really big opportunity here.
And so, um, what we're trying to do is
take this very broad advisory and
localize that for farmers. So, farmers
should plant when the soil moisture is
sufficient for germination, not just
when it rains a couple days in a row.
So, we call this time period a suitable
planting window.
And so, what you're looking at here are
three farmers, um, Mary, Rachel, and
Joseph, and um, they each have different
rainfall patterns. They have
historically different soil moisture
content and we can provide them with
different advisory today. So, whether
it's waiting for the first rains to
come, preparing when to plant, or plant
now.
And ultimately, the way that we do this
is a very simple recommendation, um, at
the output, but it combines a lot of
different signals, um, coming in. Um,
so, we look at observed rainfall, so,
what actually happened. So, we're
pulling from, um, products like TAMSAT,
which are satellite satellite derived
rainfall estimates. We're pulling from,
um, AI forecast models. So, 50-member
ensemble probabilistic forecasting from
Google, where now we can generate, um,
50 different scenarios of what's equally
likely to happen. Um, and and
ultimately, think through, um, what that
means for our confidence levels when
we're we're generating advisories. We're
looking at um 20-plus year climatology,
so the historicals of um what has
happened um in the past that can now
start helping us look beyond the
forecast window. So, 10 to 20 days out,
when forecasts are just not good enough
today, we can start to understand, well,
what was it like in that period in the
past? Then we also look at land surface
models um like Jules to understand the
soil moisture content um for these
farmers. And so, all of these models are
great, predictions are great, but we try
to calibrate them with the reality. Um
and so, we've got um what we call our
gold standard validation network, um
which is made up of hundreds of weather
stations and soil moisture probes um in
the region. And we we actually calibrate
all of these different signals in to
provide a blended estimate of when is
the best time to plant. And so, again,
it's not just when will the rains come,
but will these rains stay? Um will they
be reliable enough to give you the the
soil moisture you need to germinate your
crops.
And um all of this does not matter
unless farmers trust and act on it. And
the the critical piece for this is um
quality, accuracy, scale. And so, um we
work with a number of partners, many of
whom are in this room today from the
University of Reading, One Acre Fund, um
many government partners like the
Government of Kenya with KALRO, the
Kenya Agriculture and Livestock Research
Organization, um to to battle test and
field test these products. Um so, for
example, with uh University of Reading
and One Acre Fund, we've looked at over
80,000 um farmer trial points going
across many years and eight different
countries to look at when did farmers
plant and what was their yield. And so,
how do you correlate against historical
patterns? Um with um in-season records,
we're able to actually understand are
recommendations matching up to what
farmers are actually doing. And so, we
did a study of that with over a million
farmer records last year um in in Kenya
with KALRO. And we're also testing
everything from message design and
framing to message frequency to even
farmer demographics and typology. Like,
is this farmer a dry planter or wet
planter? That ultimately dictate whether
or not a farmer will adopt a message.
And so we've seen that farmers time and
time again who plant closer to
recommended dates achieve higher yields.
And the way that we deliver these
messages importantly matters a lot. So
it has to happen through trusted
partners. It's not Tomorrow Now sending
messages out to to farmers directly. We
actually work with a whole host of
partners.
As Zane mentioned, many of these are
public institutions, but we also work
with the private sector.
And and these messages go out to to
farmers typically once or twice a week.
And so this is actually Maggie here
again and we we had a chance to catch up
with her a few weeks ago and this is
what she told us.
If I'd planted two weeks earlier, the
soil didn't have enough water. It
wouldn't have germinated fully. I
planted at the right time and now I'm
proud to see how the crops are growing.
And so we were actually able to catch
one of those false starts with Maggie
this season in Kenya which was actually
a much trickier season than normal where
the rains did come early and that meant
very different things for many different
farmers.
And importantly Maggie's case is not
just an isolated one. So late planting
actually hits women farmers hardest. So
47% of women versus 43% of men in Kenya
plant late. And so I know that might not
appear like a huge delta, but women
smallholder farmers actually constitute
the majority of farmers in Kenya and
Africa. And and even just a small
percentage point means tens of thousands
of women farmers are planting later than
than men on average. And so when we
think about that it makes sense. Some
women are getting second access to
labor, to inputs like seeds, and then
also to information especially around
technology usage. And so our suitable
planting window model helps to close
that information gap and and get these
farmers advice at the time that they
need it so that they can make a
different decision.
And then lastly I just want to close
with
just our vision. And again it's it's a
hundred million weather resilient
farmers, but that needs to start in one
field. So, we need to look at the
behavior science um that will ultimately
result in changing um practices of when
you plant. So, we're live today with
government partners in um four
countries, in Kenya, Malawi, Zambia,
Nigeria, where we're serving over six
million farmers. We've also got a number
of private sector partnerships that take
us to a few new countries, and we're
rapidly expanding and hoping to get to
five to ten countries over the next few
years. So, our vision um is only
achieved through partnership and
thinking about the quality of these
models. Um, the AHI um based forecasting
is incredible. It's starting to increase
our confidence, starting to increase how
we actually design these messages, but
the delivery of that message um matters
just as much. And so, um at
Tomorrow.Now, we're combining both um
and bridging really this this first-mile
R&D science and AI world with the last
mile of farmer impact. And so, um yeah,
just love to take any questions, and um
I'll be around all day.
>> [applause]
>> We have uh time for probably two
questions. We can take them back to
back. Raise your hand if you have any
questions in the room.
We have one right here, Emma, right in
the middle.
And if you can uh introduce yourself and
and stand up for us uh for the cameras.
Thank you.
>> Sure, thank you. Uh Mike Sizo,
University of Maryland and NASA Harvest.
>> Cool. Um
I think one of the sort of
worries with the system like this is
that does it accurately pick up on real
local scale variability uh both in terms
of soil and in terms of like the the
accuracy of the rainfall uh product, and
does it have bias in certain areas
versus not? And I'm just wondering if
how you've seen this work based on for
that question.
Yeah, it's a great question. Um, it's
something that we think about all the
time. Um, so, one thing that we often
see people confuse um today as as
resolution with accuracy and it's very
different. So, um you know, I what we
look at right now is at a 9 km grid
level when we're providing these
advisories and I think an important
thing is not to be extremely definitive
in saying you must plant now. It's
actually that's why we've thought about
this as a suitable planting window where
we provide farmers with enough context
about the why um in terms of the
rainfall and we're actually integrating
in um sort of the best available um soil
maps. So, it's not perfect um but we are
calibrating that against what's actually
happening in the field and I think um
there is a a margin of error as well.
So, when you tell a farmer plant today,
most farmers don't plant that day. They
actually plant a few days from then um
and so it's actually trying to anchor
that point around um
around what's happening around them. So,
I think there there's a lot of variables
in there and and something that you can
always continue to improve but the
current guidance to farmers is um is
usually far from sufficient and at such
a resolution where they they can't use
it at all.
Great. We have time for one more
question.
If there is one and if there's not, I
have one.
Up.
David in the back.
Mike's coming to you right now.
Um the US funded initiative Climate
Hazards Center and also FEWS NET does a
remarkably good job of predicting rain
events months in advance. I think they
got in seven of the last eight drought
conditions in the horn accurately
predicted.
And that's a ongoing existing
investment.
What is the case you would make for
superseding that taxpayer funded
investment to this one? Why are you
better?
Yeah. Um so, in in my world, um
what we're not trying to do is supersede
anything. We're actually data and
technology agnostic. I think what we've
spent a lot of time is is building the
rails of how do you actually get this
information out to farmers at scale? Um,
so when we think about the right
partners that we work with, we actually
work with governments for a reason. They
have the mandate to reach all
smallholder farmers, not just the most
commercially viable ones. So, I think
when these types of products become
available or are available, we'd want to
integrate them in. Um, and so things
like predicting the type of season, the
characteristics of a season many months
in advance is very helpful. I think
where we're we've started with is this
real-time um weather information and how
to bring that to farmers. So, questions
around timing of when to plant is is
critical versus um you know, other
decisions like what's the best seed that
I should use, which might be better
adapt to this length of the growing
season. And so, I think there's a a role
for all of these types of innovations to
come in. And so, the way that we've
approached this is um by building what
we call our global access platform,
where we're pulling in the best-in-class
models and products from the University
of Reading, um which is around um
suitable planting windows. Or um you
know, when we look at pest and disease
advisory, working with um groups like
CABI. So, I think um yeah, we'd love to
consider working with um with that group
and and add that in. But our focus has
been how do we prove the value at scale,
and then I think you can continue to add
in new functionality.
Thank you so much. Uh join me in
thanking Brian one more time before we
move on to our next speaker.
>> [music]
